1.grade_fit_note: 'Show me. Then do it again' all but defines the word; skeptical is a common grade 4-5 context-clue word.
1.note: Sound item, key is unique. The context is so direct that it plays below grade 6; amazed and excited are the live distractors.

2.grade_fit_note: Paired commas around a nonrestrictive clause matches L.6.2a.
2.note: Clean 2x2 on the opening and closing comma. B (no commas) is the strongest distractor, since 'which' without commas is common in student writing; a restrictive reading is not credible for 'our school library'.

3.grade_fit_note: Correlative conjunctions are L.5.1e; meaning is fixed by 'so the school rented a tent'.
dimensions_varied: meaning of the correlative pair (negative / alternative / additive)
whether the pair is correctly matched (neither...or is mismatched)
3.note: B and C fail on meaning (if either room had space, no tent would be needed); D fails on form. D is a good trap for students who know the meaning but not the pairing.

4.grade_fit_note: Cause-effect transition, suitable for grade 6, perhaps on the easy side.
4.note: Instead is the live distractor because 'instead of five' appears in the sentence, but it repeats that and does not link to sentence 2. Cause-effect is clear, so it may play slightly low.

5.grade_fit_note: Direction vs. region capitalization is a standard grade 5-6 convention.
5.note: Balanced 2x2 (north/North x Midwest/midwest), no tell. The direction/region distinction trips many grade 5 students, so it probably sits a band above the stated target.

6.grade_fit_note: Avoiding pronoun shifts in person is L.6.1c/d.
6.note: Your is the realistic trap (generic-you shift); their is plausible for students who read 'coach' or 'muscles' as the antecedent. His is dead. 'We ... our' is obvious, so likely below grade 6.

7.grade_fit_note: Ambivalent is a grade 7-level Tier 2 word; context lists one positive and one negative.
7.free_elimination: B is the odd one out in form: A, C and D all have the shape 'feeling + intensifier + one emotion', while B alone is 'having mixed feelings'. A test-wise student can pick it without reading.
7.note: The content is good and nervous/upset are tempting. The format tell should be fixed by making the distractors match B's shape, e.g. 'having no strong feelings'.

8.grade_fit_note: Privilege is a classic commonly misspelled word for grades 6-8.
8.note: All three misspellings are realistic (e/i swap, inserted d). No form tell.

9.grade_fit_note: 'Taking only tiny sips' makes the meaning near-explicit.
9.note: The key is unique, but the context does nearly all the work. Leak out is the only live distractor; grow warm and taste stale do not explain the tiny sips.

10.grade_fit_note: Occurrence (double c, double r, -ence) is a grade 7-8 spelling demon.
10.note: Balanced 2x2 on c doubling x -ance/-ence, so no tell from the option set.

11.grade_fit_note: Elaborate with a list of examples suits grade 5 context clues.
11.note: Handmade is the strong distractor (true of the card, but not what the word means); costly is weaker. Format inconsistency: the passage is in the question stem but the stem says 'as it is used in the passage', and there is no separate passage block.

12.grade_fit_note: Clause function is L.7.1a; noun clause as direct object is squarely grade 7.
dimensions_varied: part of speech the clause acts as (adjective / noun / adverb)
grammatical role or what it modifies (Room 12, object of knew, subject, 'tells where')
12.note: D is a strong lure because 'where' suggests an adverb. C is dead since 'Nobody' is plainly the subject. Clause-function items usually run above grade level, so this likely plays at 210+.

13.grade_fit_note: Necessary is a standard grade 5 spelling word.
13.note: Clean 2x2 on c and s doubling. No tell.

14.grade_fit_note: Family titles after a possessive are a grade 5 capitalization skill.
14.note: Both nouns follow 'my', so both are lowercase. D (Grandma capitalized) is a strong trap because many students capitalize grandma as a name. Probably plays slightly above 180-189.

15.grade_fit_note: The '18 milliliters' figure in sentence 4 points straight to measured.
15.note: Estimated is the only real competitor, and the exact figure rules it out. Fine as a precision item, but it plays below 200.

16.grade_fit_note: Perfect verb tenses are L.5.1b/c; 'since' plus 'still' signals present perfect.
16.note: Clean 2x2 on tense and aspect. Teaches and had taught are both realistic errors.

17.note: Balanced 2x2. Theirselves and themself are real dialect or emerging forms, so all four are live, but the standard form is familiar and the item may play slightly low.

18.grade_fit_note: Meticulous with a contrast clue and an example clue suits grade 6.
18.note: Speedy is a good contrast trap (it describes Owen). Two clues (contrast plus the exact-thirds example) make it fairly easy.

19.grade_fit_note: Series commas and the comma after an introductory clause are L.5.2a/b.
19.note: Clean 2x2 (introductory comma x series commas). A is the strongest distractor.

20.grade_fit_note: Coordinate vs. cumulative adjectives is L.7.2a.
20.note: Clean 2x2 on 'long, boring' and 'new, winter'. C is the over-comma trap and is attractive.

21.grade_fit_note: 'Nobody repaired ... for years' plus 'replace them' makes the meaning near-explicit.
21.note: The key is unique, but the context gives it away; squeak, dry out and slippery are weak lures because none of them alone forces closing and replacing boards. A grade 7 word with grade 6 difficulty.

22.grade_fit_note: Misplaced and dangling modifiers are L.7.1c.
22.free_elimination: D splits the verb from its object ('carried, ... the pizza'), which sounds wrong to any native-level reader without any grammar knowledge.
dimensions_varied: position of the participial phrase (after object / sentence-initial / sentence-final / between verb and object)
which noun the phrase ends up modifying (pizza / Marco / table or Marco)
22.note: B (a dangling modifier, with Marco dripping) is the classic lure; C reads as the table or Marco dripping. D is effectively dead, so this is really a three-option item.

23.grade_fit_note: Languages are capitalized and school subjects are not, a standard grade 6 convention.
23.note: Balanced 2x2. B (Science capitalized) is the strong trap.

24.grade_fit_note: Historical events are capitalized and centuries are not, a grade 7 convention.
24.note: Balanced 2x2. D is a strong trap because 'Nineteenth Century' looks like a proper name.
